newsitem.title: THAILAND: Moody's review seen negative for Thai markets.
newsitem.headline: Moody's review seen negative for Thai markets.

text.p: Rating agency Moody's announcement of a possible downgrade of Thailand long-term foreign currency debt ceilings would add further pressure on Thailand's weak stock market and baht, analysts said on Friday.

"This will add more pressure on the weakening baht. An expected rise in local interest rates will also have further effect on the stock market," Darunee Ithiputh, general manager of foreign exchange for Hong Kong-based Perigrine Fixed Income Ltd told Reuters.
Moody's Investors Service said on Friday that it had placed the A2 foreign-currency sovereign ceilings for bonds and bank deposits of Thailand on review for possible downgrade.

The agency said that the review was prompted by concerns over the soundness of Thailand's financial sector, in which a large portion of the recent accumulation of short-term foreign curency debt had been concentrated. It was also worried by constraints on macroeconomic policy-making.
Moody's review of Thailand's long-term foreign debt set off a 4.53 percent plunge on the Thai stock index, and the baht weakened as well, brokers and dealers said.
Moody's last September cut Thailand's short-term sovereign ceiling ratings for bank deposits and other short-term obligations to Prime 2 from Prime 1.
The baht was below 26 to the dollar and bid/offer was quoted at 26.060-26.080 around 0625 GMT.

Thai money and stock markets have been hit hard in past weeks by rumours of an imminent baht devaluation and the maintenance of high domestic interest rates by the central bank to keep the currency attractive, analysts said.
Rumours of a liquidity crunch affecting some financial institutions and a sluggish economy have added to problems.

"At the moment, the sentiment of the Thai financial market is particulary weak," said Desmond Supple, senior emerging economist at the Singapore-based research house, I.D.E.A. "If we throw the issue of a potential downgrade into the melting pot, then it could be disastrous."

The possible downgrade of Thailand's long-term foreign debt would also raise the cost of offshore borrowings by Thai corporations and financial institutions and cause an outflow of foreign funds, analysts said.

"So far, I haven't seen major capital flight from Thailand. If Moody's really downgrades (Thailand's long-term rating), the substantial outflow of foreign funds is likely," Darunee at Perigrine Fixed Income said.
Analysts said the Bank of Thailand had to implement more strict measures to curb foreign borrowing which is a major worry behind Moody's possible downgrade.
"More needs to be done. The Bank of Thailand has been lax on this issue," Supple said.
